The recommendation with respect to procedure on divorce bills is the best that the committee could evolve, having regard to the limited length of time we devoted to a discussion of the subject. I support that recommendation and I ask hon. members of the house to support it, but it is not dealing with the problem as it ought to be dealt with.
This is the suggestion I make to the government. Get this vexed question of divorce, out of the arena of parliamentary government. Get it out of the Senate and get it out of the House of Commons. Let us set up a division of the Exchequer Court of Canada, a division which will be clothed with jurisdiction to deal with divorce. We can do this, and then let us relegate the whole question of divorce to the courts, where it ought to be, just as we have referred the question of contested elections to the courts. It will not take away from us our right to deal with the question of divorce by legislation. Neither have we by referring contested elections to the courts robbed parliament of its jurisdiction to deal with that subject. Parliament right down through the ages has decided that questions of the kind which involve judicial discretion and that sort of thing can best be dealt with by the courts. My recommendation to the Prime Minister and to the government and to the members of the house, and may I say with the utmost candour to those who perhaps differ with me as to the ethical or religious aspects involved, that I believe the proper course for them to support would be to get this vexed question out of parliament and into the hands of a judicial body which will approach it fully qualified by education and by administrative experience and by knowledge of the law and of procedure to deal with it in a judicial manner. I commend that to the whole house. Let us not pussyfoot with this question any longer. Let us have an expression of opinion, if you like, although I am not inviting extensive debate; let us try to do something constructive in the matter and get this question off the order paper once and for all.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I understand that the various recommendations made by the committee will be discussed in the order in which they were made and will be decided by a vote of this committee. I do not therefore think it is necessary to take very much time in a general discussion. To do so, I think, would be to act contrary to the

purpose for which the committee was set up. I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in what he said about the committee. I was very glad to find that all its members, regardless of what party or group they belonged, were equally determined that the rights of the minorities should be maintained. In that connection, I think, we also recognized that the minority rights were not rights of groups only, but were rights of individuals. As has been very well put into the report by those who drafted it- Votes and Proceedings page 147:
It is in truth the privilege of their constituents and it is secured to members not for their personal benefit but to enable them to discharge the functions of their office.
That is the spirit in which the committee approached its work. There may be a feeling, possibly a justifiable one, that the committee did not go sufficiently deep into the rules of procedure and bring in a fuller report-that is, a report proposing changes which would expedite the business of the house to the extent that we think it should be expedited. But the committee felt that we were dealing with the subject at an abnormal time. This is a time of war, when ordinary parliamentary procedure is, necessarily, upset, and we grant to the government, because of the necessities of the times, many powers which would not be given to it in ordinary times. I believe that when we return again to normal conditions a similar committee should be set up to go more fully into the rules.
There is another point which the committee had in mind. While we tried to maintain and were anxious to maintain the rights of minorities, we realized that there is such a thing as the rights of the majority; that the government, after what might be considered sufficient time has been given to debate any matter, must have resources to curtail debate and get on with the business which has been entrusted to it by the country.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury referred to the necessity of preserving the dignity of the House of Commons. I think we are all agreed on that. But after all, the people of the country want something more than dignity; they expect parliament to do business, and I believe business can be done just as well in a dignified as in an undignified way. But let us not lose sight of the fact that the people of the country to-day have come very close to parliament. When parliamentary institutions were in process of growth, parliament had very little to do with the everyday life of the people. Parliament was a Sort of policeman; it arranged for granting the ruling monarch money to run the country, and concerned itself with a limited range of things of that kind. But to-day

Rules of the House
parliament is concerned with the everyday life of the people in an intimate way, and all are agreed that in future it will be more concerned with that than it has been in the past or is even to-day.
If we are to be successful in carrying on with our democratic institutions, something more than standing orders and rules will be necessary. Democracy in the ultimate depends on self-discipline, and I believe we can promote that' practice here in the House of Commons. The government of the day could facilitate and speed the work of the house and obtain cooperation from the opposition by approaching the opposition in a spirit of cooperation, but it will have to be done in such a way as to satisfy the opposition that the government has nothing "up its sleeve," as the saying is. I am satisfied that if the opposition is approached in this way a great deal can be accomplished. Perhaps the reason I lean so definitely in that direction is that I myself am a cooperative person; I hate to be driven, but I respond quickly to cooperation, and I find that that is also true of the people with whom I am associated.
There are one or two recommendations with which I do not fully agree, and I shall have something to say on those as they come up, so that I will not at this point take any further time of the committee.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
As one who sat on the committee I should like to say that I appreciated the expeditious way in which, under the able chairmanship of Mr. Speaker, it concluded its sittings. I suppose some hon. members will feel that the committee did not go far enough, and I do not doubt that a good deal of criticism in that regard will be heard from people outside the house. On the other hand there will doubtless be many hon. members who believe that the report goes too far.
I believe we all agree it is desirable that measures be introduced with a view to expediting the business of the house. We have all been aware that business has on occasions dragged on day after day without anything really worth while being accomplished. On the other hand we all agree that the rights and privileges of individual members and of minorities must be guarded jealously. So that when you try to expedite the business of the house without infringing upon the rights of individual members or minorities, you face a difficult problem. These points were plainly in the minds of the committee during its sittings.
As I understand that the different sections will be taken one at a time, I will conclude by saying that, generally speaking, I am in full accord with the report.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I want to make a few remarks concerning the amendment proposed to the parliamentary rules and forms of the House of Commons. It was a real pleasure and satisfaction for me and my colleagues to hear a few moments ago the speech delivered by His Honour the Speaker. Elected to this house in 1925, I remember that His Honour was at that time, as he has been at all times, one of the best debaters in this house. Mr. Speaker is now speaking with the same eloquence.
(Translation):	Generally speaking, the
proposed amendments to the Rules of the House are excellent. However, I am bound to oppose one of them, for it is detrimental to the rights and privileges of members of this house. Why should the support of twenty members, instead of five as heretofore, be necessary in the future to force a vote on a decision of the hon. Speaker? This is a harsh proposition which should not go through. Thus, when a minority group numbers less than 20 members, it will be impossible for them to force a vote without the support of members from other groups with political tenets inconsistent with their own. In most cases it will be absolutely impossible. Such a measure would deprive the representatives of the people of the freedom of speech to which they are entitled in moving amendments to government policies. Indeed, what would be the use of moving such amendments if those members are deprived of the privilege of forcing a vote on a decision of the hon. Speaker, due to conditions which render the taking of a vote an impossibility?
I am not finding fault with the other proposed amendments. On the contrary, they will result in shortening the debate, especially in connection with the estimates. Mr. Chairman, measures should have been adopted long ago to curb the abuses that have been so common at every session of parliament, when the estimates are before the house. I have seen members repeatedly taking part in the debate on a single item, making the same utterances ten and even fifteen times over. At last, the government realize the futility of such goings on, which unduly lengthen the sessions of parliament.
I shall close my remarks by a few words on the divorce bills. The * committee entrusted with the revision of the Rules of the House have recommended some amendments which would render the adoption of divorce bills more difficult. I congratulate them for it. I shall go further and state that divorce bills should not be submitted either to the house or
Rules of the House

to a committee of the house. When such bills apply to Roman Catholics or when one of the parties is a Catholic, the bills should simply be dropped.
The civil code of the province of Quebec contains measures entitling the interested parties to apply to the courts of the province for an action in separation from bed and board or a decree of invalidity in certain special cases. Therefore, I wonder why the federal government does not adopt an act to refer Catholic husbands and wives to our courts, where they could avail themselves of French civil laws. Besides, the Roman Catholic dogmas hold that marriage is indissoluble and that its bonds can be severed only by the death of one of the parties. The federal government, when adopting divorce bills concerning Catholic married couples residing in the province of Quebec, not only transgresses against the civil code of that province, but also violates Canon law and the precepts of the Catholic faith.
One further remark, Mr. Chairman. The granting of these divorce bills, like a cancerous growth, eats into the very life of society, of which the family is the living cell. Divorce is one of the worst evils of our days. It should once for all be banished from civilization. It is a disgrace for both parents and children. The government is contemplating the implementation of a complete programme of social legislation. Will they allow divorce to keep on eating away at the very heart of1 society, the family? We claim to be fighting for civilization and still we adopt divorce bills worthy of Zulus and of the most backward tribes of the universe. Why not, once for all, close the doors of parliament against these divorce bills which have done us and are still doing us so much harm? Thus we would protect parents against themselves and children against the deplorable errors of their elders. This is a social as well as a national duty. The government must not and cannot avoid the issue. On behalf of family, society and civilization, I urge that divorce, this canker of society and the home, be prohibited.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I have had the pleasure and honour of serving on two committees while a member of this house, which committees were set up to consider the rules and standing orders of the house. As the hon. member for York^unbury (Mr. Hanson) said, he was on the committee in 1927 and I [Mr. Lacombe.j
had the honour of being on that same committee. The late Speaker Lemieux was chairman of that committee, as our Speaker to-day is chairman of the committee which has brought in this report.
I do not think any member of the committee would pretend to ask the house to accept the report as a complete solution of all the problems that arise from time to time in procedure in this House of Commons, but I hope the house generally will feel that some improvement is offered by the report in this respect.
I do not propose to go into the report in detail, but I would refer to two or three of the proposed amendments. For instance, standing order 37 now Teads:
No member, except the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, or a minister moving a government order and the member speaking in reply immediately after such minister, or a member making a motion of "no. confidence" in the government and a minister replying thereto, shall speak for more than forty minutes at a time in any debate.
That forty-minute limitation applies not only when the Speaker is in the chair but in committee as well. As has been pointed out by previous speakers, any member in committee of the whole can make as many forty minute speeches as he likes, and, the afternoon session lasting only three hours, two or three members can take up the whole time of the house. It is with a view to improving that condition that this amendment is offered as section 2 of standing order 37, in these words:
Provided always that in committees of the whole, supply or ways and means, no member shall speak more than once on a particular motion, clause or item under consideration, and not more than twenty minutes continuously, but his right to ask questions relating to the subject matter of the said motion, clause or item under consideration shall not be thereby restricted.
To some extent that does cut down the time that a member may take up in committee, but I do not think it takes away any substantial rights that he may enjoy as a private member of the house.
The proposed amendment to section 2 of standing order 43 in effect adds to the rights of a minister of the crown as the rules now stand. That section reads:
A reply shall be allowed to a member who has moved a substantive motion, but not to the mover of an amendment, the previous question or an instruction to a committee.

Rules of the House
It ia now proposed that the following words be added:
... or the second reading of a bill, and to a minister of the crown who has introduced a government measure.
Once a minister has introduced a government measure, criticism or commendation is offered, and it seemed to the committee only right that the minister should have the privilege of replying to all that had been said regarding that measure, though under the rules as they are constituted at present he has not that right.
Then a recommendation is made in regard to questions asked on the orders of the day, which I know have been a source of worry, shall I say, to all Speakers of this house. The committee did not see fit to curtail the right of hon. members to ask questions of ministers on the orders of the day, and in that I heartily concur; but following the British practice it was thought that the procedure might be improved, and the committee has proposed that the following be added as section 5 of standing order 44:
A question of urgent character may he addressed orally to a minister on the orders of the day being called, provided a copy thereof has been delivered to the minister and to the Clerk of the House at least one hour before the meeting of the house. Such a question shall not be prefaced by the reading of telegrams, newspaper extracts, letters or preambles of any kind. The answer shall be oral and may be immediately followed by supplementary questions limited to three in number, without debate or comment, for the elucidation of the information given by the minister.
I hope the government will approve this recommendation, and that it will meet with the support of hon. members of the house.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the moment I do not intend to comment on the recommendations that have been presented by this committee. Rather I should like to direct attention to another recommendation which in my opinion would be very desirable but which the committee has not seen fit to. include in its report. Citation 314 under standing order 41 reads:
It is a rule in both houses of parliament that a member must address the house orally, and not read from a written, previously prepared speech, for the reason that "if the practice of reading speeches should prevail, members might read speeches that were written by other people, and the time of the house be taken up in considering the arguments of persons who were not deserving of their attention."
It has been the custom of a great many hoa. members of this house to read their speeches, though roughly and freely; and when no objection has been taken Mr. Speaker has allowed
them to continue to do so. Unfortunately, however, some of those who usually read their own speeches would object to other hon. members being given the same privilege. In. my view this situation should be settled, and I had hoped that the committee might recommend that standing order 41 be done away with altogether, or on the other hand that the rule be applied strictly to all hon-. members of the house.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is some seventeen years since the rules of the house were last amended. I have been a member of the house since 1930, and before we go on to deal with the individual recommendations I should like to say a word or two in general. First, in reference to the remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), it is my opinion that hon. members did not send in suggestions to the special committee because we all realized that the committee was composed of members experienced in the rules of procedure; and speaking for myself, I felt that I could not make any suggestion of which the members of the special committee would not have personal knowledge already. As the hon. member for York-Sunbury was speaking, however, I noted his reference to the support he gave to the proposal that in committee of the' whole members should be limited to twenty minutes. If my timing was accurate the hon. member took a little over twenty minutes this afternoon, which indicates to me at least that we should be very careful not to change these rules too quickly .because in so doing perhaps we may shut off an hon. member who has something really worth while to say.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) pointed out that we are at war, that certain changes are necessary during war time, and that after the war is over we might go back to the old rules. Well, Mr. Chairman, I -am not as sanguine as the hon. member "is in that regard, because every change that has been made in the past in regard to the rules has remained in effect. The fact that it is some seventeen years since the rules have been changed shows at least how reluctant we are to alter the rules which have to do with the conduct of the House of Commons. Very few hon. members have made a study of the rules, but I think most of us have at least a sense of what they should be, realizing that after all we have an important position to uphold and that we should set an example in decorum and good behaviour.
The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) had a word to say with regard to the reading of speeches. I trust that what I am about
Rules of the House

to say will not be taken as a reflection upon the present Speaker or upon any hon. member of this house, because that is not my intention; but the reading of speeches has been a very sore point, shall I say, with many members of parliament. I am one of those who take the position that while there is a duty imposed upon members of this house to uphold the rules, there is also a duty upon those who conduct the proceedings of the house or the committee. The duties of members of the house are well expressed in the report brought down, where it is stated that-
Rules are not sufficient to preserve freedom of speech and to uphold the dignity of the House of Commons. Standing orders depend for their success upon the prevalence of good will amongst all members who have to -work under them. The house must rely on the forbearance of its members and on the general acquiescence in the enforcement by the Speaker of the rule -which requires that members should strictly confine themselves to matters immediately pertinent to the subject of debate.
That is all very true. When I first came to the House of Commons, like most new members I felt rather timid and on that occasion attempted to read my speech. But I had a difficult time in getting through, because one hon. member on the government side-we were sitting in opposition at the time-drew Mr. Speaker's attention to the fact that I w^as reading my speech; and the then Speaker, the present hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black), rose I believe something like five times in an endeavour to have me desist from reading my speech. I shall not forget the example set for me on that occasion. It was a good lesson to me. I had come to the chamber with my speech fully written out, as a new member of the house. Had I been stopped on that occasion from reading I must confess the speech might not have been delivered. Perhaps it does not matter now whether it was delivered or not. The fact is that I was stopped. I did feel it keenly when, after that, I saw other hon. members deliberately reading their speeches. No member with any great sense of feeling likes to rise in his place and draw Mr. Speaker's attention to the fact that another hon. member is reading his speech. I did not do it then, although I might well have done it; and had I wanted to get back at members on the government side, I had reason to do it. I personally object to the reading of speeches; it is a dangerous procedure which has grown up in our House of Commons. I say at once that a well-read speech, if it is a good one, is much better than one which is not well delivered and may not contain as much good material, but 
it is better that the member express his own thoughts. After all however we had better be careful that we do not countenance the thoughts and mind of someone outside the house. It is the easiest thing in the world for individuals belonging to any party, or for independents or the members of any group, to have speeches deliberately written for them and handed to them when they are entering the house. It is very easy to read those speeches. I do not say this in any spirit of criticism, but I do believe we are drifting toward the American system, where members may hand in a whole speech. One of them, I believe, handed in the whole Book of Isaiah.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: That would be at least better than the speeches.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I offer that as an illustration to show to what extent the reading of speeches has progressed across the boundary line, and how we are drifting in that direction. As was pointed out by the then Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, it is not a good thing to introduce the 246th member into the house, when there are only 245 places.
I shall leave that part of my remarks by saying this, that I for one believe that the rules should be strictly enforced on everyone alike. I believe that in that event every hon. member will not object, believing that the rules offer ample assurance that every one of us may speak, no matter on which side of the house he may sit. All hon. members realize that we must have rules in the house, just the same as does a ratepayers' association, if it is to run its own show with decency and decorum. We would have bedlam and confusion on many occasions if half a dozen hon. members were trying to speak without having the rules brought into effect.
May I now return to one of the provisions in the suggested rules to which I think I shall have to take exception at the proper time. I refer to the suggested rule that a member may speak only once for twenty minutes continuously when the house is in committee of supply or ways and means. If that means that an hon. member may sf>eak only once on an item, whether it be for five minutes or twenty minutes, and that following that his right is only that of asking questions, I must oppose it. I would ask hon. members to give serious consideration to this suggestion. If it means something other than I have described, the wording is not clear. I shall not read the paragraph now, because we shall reach it later in the debate. I would view with alarm, however, any curtailment of the rights of members.

Rules of the House
I know that at times we refer to what takes place in Great Britain. But after all, the people of Great Britain are different from us. Their philosophy goes back hundreds of years and, more or less, they are all the same kind of people. On the other hand we are a new country to which people have come from all other countries of the world.
There are some who hold the view which I deprecate, that ability to speak is the sole indication of ability. I contend that is not always so, because many I have heard who have ability to speak had nothing much left of ability after they had spoken. We are living in days of public speaking. Every man in public life to-day must be able to hold forth. I remember a certain person being referred to as a Moses who would lead the people out of the wilderness. I said to the person who had made the reference, "I wonder . if you have read Holy Writ." You will find that when the man Moses was chosen to lead the children of Israel out of the wilderness his first remark to the Lord was, "0 my Lord,
I am not a speaker." The Lord in reply said, "I am not looking for a speaker; I am looking for a leader. We will get someone else to speak." All leaders in those days were chosen as such, but to-day our philosophy is different, and I do not know that it is all for the better.
I shall take these amendments into consideration, but I am afraid I shall have to vote against the limitation respecting the twenty-minute speech, if it means that a member cannot speak more than once on one item. Suppose a member is speaking on a certain item, and someone across the floor makes observations which should be answered; if the original speaker is confined to twenty minutes and has already used that time, he is denied the right to reply. Certainly I am not in favour of that, and I would ask hon. members to be careful how they vote when that amendment is before them.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,, I pay
tribute to Mr. Speaker and to his predecessor, who is now one of our esteemed colleagues in the house, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black), and to all 'hon. members of the committee for the work they have done. I pay tribute, too, to hon. members who have already spoken in a non-partisan spirit.
I have read the report carefully, and it reminds me of a remark once made to me by a learned theologian, a holy man who had listened to a sermon delivered by a young clergyman. I noticed the theologian was walking in the corridor and counting on his fingers. Afterwards I said to him, "Did you pray during the sermon?" He said, "No, I was
counting the heresies." If we read the preamble of the report we find there are many statements which stare at each other and put us under the obligation of accepting the report, not with a grain but with a pail of salt.	[DOT]
The first sentence reads:
Your committee, in the performance of the important duty assigned to it by the house, has taken into account the existence of general criticism of parliament both by members and representative citizens.
Whoever heard of general criticism of parliament, even by the press? There have been some tycoons who have tried to impose their views upon parliament, who have tried to discredit the work of members of parliament, but that is all. I should like the members of the press gallery to change places with us some day and let us pass judgment upon their work. I think they would find it pretty hard to do what hon. members are doing, not only for their constituents but for the Canadian people at large.
My first observation is that this report has been actuated by fear-fear of the yellow press and of certain club men who know nothing about what is going on in parliament but who pass judgment upon us while smoking long cigars between drinks of Scotch and soda. I deny most emphatically that there has been a general criticism of parliament, especially by members of parliament. For a member to do that would be for him to prove himself unfaithful to his colleagues. He would be forgetting the work that they are actually doing in this house for the Canadian people. If there has been criticism by representative citizens, it has been by only a handful of men who do not know what they are talking about.
The report goes on:
It has been fully realized that much is expected of the House of Commons where the views of the people are finding expression and where industrial and economic conditions are demanding parliamentary attention and solution.
Mark you, those are the words of an optimist. When have we been able to solve industrial and economic problems? We are called here simply to vote money and impose taxation. That is the only thing we have done since the beginning of the war. The report goes on:
The main question before the committee was whether procedure should be amended so that the house may be able to do more legislative work in the time at its disposal and increase its efficiency as a critical and controlling assembly.
We must read between the lines. In the first place, it is not the business of hon. members to initiate legislation; that is the duty of
Rules of the House

the government. A private member may introduce legislation, but it never gets beyond the second reading. Private members cannot be blamed if the legislation is not satisfactory. This part of the report is a reflection upon the kind of legislation that has been brought before the house by the government. It cannot be otherwise, because we are precluded from bringing in legislation. I quote again:
-and increase its efficiency as a critical and controlling assembly.
Note those words, "controlling assembly." That means the controlling of accounts, but we have no accounts. How can we control accounts that we do not have? Year after year I have insisted upon the reestablishment of the old system of accounting, and where did I get any support? I received some support from two of my friends in the Conservative party, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). I also received some encouragement from the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), the leader of the New Democracy group. I admit that the former leader of the opposition agreed' with me and with the other hon. members whom I have mentioned already, but he said we should wait until after the war to see to>
it. He admitted that the complaint was well-founded but thought it would be in the public interest to wait until after the war when we could discuss the whole thing.
There was a third point of view expressed by a member of the Conservative party. It was put forth by one of the members from Toronto who said that I was playing Hitler's game when I was doing some work for my own constituents and for the Canadian people. I was simply asking for information. That statement was made in plain language by one of the members from Toronto whom I would name if he were in his seat at the present time. It is pretty hard to be doing something in this house for the Canadian people and then be treated in that way by one of my colleagues. There is something lacking in this report. It should contain a provision to permit you to call to order any member who accuses any one of his colleagues of doing something to help the enemy when he is just trying to defend his own people. The report continues:
_ Criticisms of parliament seem to have been inadequately considered in relation to the whole structure of parliament, the necessary party system and the complex situation created by a war which is now in its fifth year.
And later on:
Parliament is the assembly of representatives elected by the people where great issues are 
debated, or should be debated; it is not primarily a body of auditors charged with the inspection of departmental accounts.
Two of those statements contradict each other. One states that the House of Commons is a controlling assembly and the other states that we are not a body of auditors. How is it possible to reconcile those two statements? I have referred to the attempts I have made to have proper public accounts and a proper report by the auditor general brought before us. Every cent expended by the treasury should be accounted for. What do we get? Practically nothing. The right of audit, which is the right of parliament has been taken over by the Department of Finance, by the comptroller of the treasury. The Minister of Finance alone has the right to approve the payment of items voted for any department. He is empowered with the right to audit those payments. The office of the auditor general has become just a mockery. I quote:
Freedom of speech is one of the inalienable privileges of members of the House of Commons. It is in truth the privilege of their constituents-
That is false. It is true to a certain extent, but it is not complete. We are not here only to represent our constituents. We are here, each one of us, to represent the Canadian people at large. And how does it work? It is very easy to understand. We are passing legislation that applies to every citizen of this country. Therefore a member of parliament does not represent only his constituents. A member of parliament, every one of us, down to the last man on the last row just as much as the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, represents the whole Canadian people at large. The report goes on:
The present procedure was devised to reflect the freedom of all the members of the house, but we must realize that in wartime parliament is bound to divest itself of some of its prerogatives in order to strengthen the government's power.
I am against it. I am against it for a very simple reason. It is that the power of the government is entirely different from the power of parliament. The power of the government, according to the British North America Act, is an executive power, and the power of parliament is a legislative power. The power of government is executive, the duty of the privy council being to execute the legislation passed by parliament. Therefore the suggestion in the report is contrary to the spirit of the constitution. I do not see how we can delegate our legislative powers to the government, although the thing is done. I know very well that the courts will support

Rules of the House
our one-man legislation passed by controllers of every description on account of the war. Nevertheless it is legally unsound. We cannot so delegate our powers as a parliament. By virtue of the constitution the government has the right to execute the legislative authority. But there is an old principle that is known by everybody. It is an old Latin axiom which is part of the Roman law. It is known not only to lawyers but to every man with the slightest touch of education. It is delegatus non potest delegare-a delegate cannot delegate again. But this is what has been done. We have so much external legislation passed at the present time, passed outside of parliament, in every war department, that it is impossible for any single member to read and check it all. There is no student of law to-day in any university who could pass an examination on constitutional or administrative law, taking into account all the orders that have been passed by dollar-a-year men.
There is something in this report that I do not understand at all. It says:
The principle of majority rule is a constitutional convention upon which all British parliamentary government is built but this must collapse in proportion as the principle of the protection of minorities begins to decay.
There are some philosophical considerations, and then we come to another contradictory statement in the report:
Your committee, in all its deliberations, has kept in mind the importance of not impairing the rights of minorities.
For otherwise, the principle of the protection of minorities "begins to decay", to use the words of the report. It goes on:
Two fundamental principles govern the procedure of the house. They are, that the government shall, so long as it can maintain a majority, be able to secure such legal flowers as it considers necessary for administration

That again is wrong, for the reasons I have already mentioned. My contention is that we cannot transfer any legal powers to the government. It goes on:
-and that minorities, however small, shall be able to criticize that administration. Standing orders must protect them, and it is all the more important that they be founded on right and justice-
Why?
-because they are merely resolutions of the house which can be swept away by a majority vote.
Is it not absurd, Mr. Chairman? The standing orders must be founded on right and justice, it says, because they are merely resolutions of the house which can be swept away
by a majority vote. That is why they are founded on right and justice. Again, the report says:
Your committee is of the firm opinion that these rights cannot be alienated even if the house, in maintaining them, may protract sessions and lay itself open to severe criticism.
They are ready to accept criticism now.
Fourteen recommendations are made by the committee. The first one is that one day a week be devoted to supply. Most of our time here, when we are not busy passing tax legislation, is devoted to a discussion of the estimates of the war departments. We have had twenty-six sitting days since the beginning of the session. The address was voted on the eleventh day, and from then on the house has considered only war estimates.
The second recommendation has to do with the suggestion of the allotment of a certain number of days for debates, with a view to saving time. The report says:
Our recommendation is that, when there is reason to believe that debate will be protracted, parties and groups recognized in the house shall confer and make arrangements either for allot-' ting days or laying any plan for saving time whilst protecting freedom of speech for every representative of the people who sits in this house.
It is doubtful how that would work. Theoretically the right of speech is the right of every hon. member, but a large number of members never exercise that right, and never will even with a change in the rules.
The third point mentioned by the committee was not a recommendation but an observation that war business has priority, and therefore government business has priority over private members' bills. Well, nobody will quarrel with that.
There is mention of the standing orders, and that there are 95 in the English house today. Once a member of the New Zealand parliament remarked to me, "What is the use of bothering about the rules of the house? There .are none." In fact, parliamentary practice is the common law of parliament; and parliamentary practice, which is based on the rulings of the Speakers, being a composite picture of all their rulings, is the best commentary on the standing orders.
We now come to the matter of compulsory voting. Why should we be forced to vote? Sometimes a member will not agree with either of two contradictory propositions. For a long time it has been the practice to allow members the freedom of voting or not voting when Mr. Speaker was in the house. I remember that on one occasion, when some hon. members refrained from voting, they had to leave the chamber when the matter was dis-
Rules of the House

cussed afterwards, but they were told that they were right, that nothing could force them to vote. I am against compulsion. If an hon. member is present and is dissatisfied with any proposal emanating from the government or from any private member, I do not see why he should be told to go out of the chamber, to go behind, the curtain, to hide himself, instead of exercising his right to remain here and not to vote. *
Then as to the appeal from Mr. Speaker's ruling, it is now proposed1 that the house shall divide only if division is demanded by twenty members. This is in, contradiction of the proposal for compulsqry voting. There is the further proposal that there shall be no appeal from Mr. Speaker's ruling. My object is not at all to cast any reflection on the ' wisdom of Mr. Speaker, but it is of the utmost importance to have the votes recorded in this house. Sometimes members speak in one way in the house and speak differently before their constituents. It is a very good thing that they should be on record as to, what they think is the best policy to follow. It should be an easy procedure to appeal from Mr. Speaker's ruling-not to cast any aspersion on his wisdom, which I recognize and to which I pay tribute, but just to, show where hon. members stand on matters of public interest.
Then there is the proposed amendment of standing order 37, relating to the number of times a member may speak in committee. As all hon. members enjoy the same rights, I do not see why any difference should be made between the right of any one and any other. In all fairness, what is good- for one hon. member, even though he be a cabinet minister, should be good for any other hon. member. Why should there be any exception to, the rule governing the time for speeches? I will go, further. If the length of a speech were curtailed to ten minutes to each member, I should have no objection, provided that cabinet ministers and private members were treated alike. I do not see why there should be any objection to that. Moreover,
I recognize that when we go into committee it is largely to ask questions of the minister in charge of the department concerned. It is said that there will be no restriction on the right of any hon. member to ask questions. But then we should come to an understanding that, when a member has a series of questions to ask a minister, nobody shall intervene to change the course of the interrogator; the member should be able during five, ten or twenty minutes to go on asking questions. But it is not so long ago-this was not under the present chairman, but one of his 
predecessors-that I was told from the Chair that when we were in committee we were there to make speeches, not to ask questions. I suffered very much at the time, and I got some experience which it is hard to forget.
Then there is something in the report about "tedious repetition". Well, this is governed by the law of relativity; it is dependent upon who is in the chair. I admire your patience, sir; I admire that of Mr. Speaker; but there have been sometimes in the chair gentlemen who were greedy for plums and who were ready to find everything tedious which was keeping the plum away. I respect very highly, sir, your wisdom and that of Mr. Speaker. But what happened in the past may happen in the future, and if we do not suffer from it now, other hon. members may suffer from it in the future, and it is our duty to protect them as best we can.	.
Then there is the matter of an amendment to a motion. I have just noted the fifth and the seventh recommendations-no appeal from Mr. Speaker's decision, but on the other hand, compulsory voting. How do they work together? It is most contradictory; it is illogical. On the one hand the report recommends compulsory voting, and afterwards it says that it is a bad thing because we shall not vote to appeal from Mr. Speaker's ruling. How many people composed that report without talking to each other before passing it over? It cannot work. If one thing is good, the other is bad. If compulsory voting is accepted there should also be an easy appeal from Mr. Speaker's ruling.
Then there is a reference to the fact that South Africa has abolished the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. That is their business. Here an opportunity is given to members of all parties to express their views at the beginning of the session, to lay before the house the complaints of their constituents, and to say whether their constituents are satisfied or dissatisfied. That is their business and it is a very good thing because it gives the government a bird's-eye view of the Canadian people.
The question is not whether a member shall be able to make a speech that can be printed at the printing bureau and sent to his constituents as a masterpiece that will be translated two thousand years hence. That is not the question. The point is that a member comes here and informs the government and his colleagues of what has been going on, to his knowledge, since the last time parliament was assembled.
There is a proposed amendment, with regard to resolutions or votes in the house,

Rules of the House
that the procedure shall be simplified. When we have resolutions for the expenditure of money amounting to billions of dollars they are worthy of consideration, and it is precisely those men who complain about us in the yellow press, who complain about members who do their duty in this house, who complain afterwards about taxes. Well, we discuss the cause of taxation and it seems to me that in dqbate the cause deserves as much consideration' as the effect.
There is a recommendation concerning divorce bills. I object to the discussion of divorce bills in this house and also very strongly to their publication in the statute books, and the sooner parliament gets rid of divorce legislation the better.
Before closing my remarks I should like to quote from the report of 1925 on the rules of the house. The second paragraph of the preliminary note reads:
Your committee has adhered to the principle that the greatest freedom be allowed the house in both its debates and proceedings. Factors tending to restrict liberty have been eliminated. The tendency has been to restrict the number of rules and reduce them to a minimum, with the object that only absolutely necessary rules be enforced, so that the house will be more particularly guided by the general principles followed in British legislative assemblies and familiar to parliamentarians in Great Britain and the self-governing dominions.
That is a very fine statement of what should be the application of the standing orders in this house. There should be no atmosphere in this house. Of course, it is impossible to prevent it by standing orders; but how many times has not cowardice been imputed to members just because they were doing their duty in the House of Commons? It will be recalled that many times members of the government have risen in protest when complaints have been made against civil servants who were usurping the rights of parliament, who were more powerful than the Prime Minister, who had a salary that was twice that of the Prime Minister, men who were considered indispensable and untouchable, not in the Hindu sense of the word, but in the sense that it is impossible to criticize them, that they are high above criticism. I did criticize them, however, when the former government was in power, and I deny anyone the right to prevent me from doing so at any time.
Let me say this to the government, as a Liberal member of old standing who is true to the principles that he has preached since he went into politics years ago, which he preached at a meeting at which Sir Wilfrid Laurier was present and also in numerous other campaigns, on the side of the Prime Minister and on the
side of the late Mr. Lapointe and other members of the Liberal party: I believe in liberty, and I believe in liberty for all.
