speechtext:
To the
detriment of all other parts of the country. If by the operations of this bank we can assist in the decentralization of industry I give it all the blessings I am capable of giving. It may do a lot of good in that respect. I have always thought that the progress of amalgamation of industry in this country was against sound public policy. I have recognized too, I have been obliged to recognize, that one of the chief factors in the amalgamation of industry in Canada was geography. You cannot beat geography. Take the cotton textile business in this country; review its history. I recall away back in the 1880's, when I was a little boy, there were established in New Brunswick no fewer than four cotton mills, all established by private capital. One of them is closed, and the other three are in the hands of a large textile company in central Canada. What was the reason for that? Principally geography. They were manufacturing raw materials that were not indigenous to this country. That may have been a mistake to start with. They had to haul the raw material from New Orleans into New Brunswick and haul the finished product into Ontario and Quebec where the density of population was, with the result that transportation costs throttled in a large measure that type of industry.
Geography is something one cannot get over. An honest attempt was made by this government in the 1920's to overcome in a degree the handicap of geography by the introduction of the Maritimes Freight Rates Act. That
1270 .
Industrial Development Bank

has been a help in maintaining such industries as we have to-day. But it has been only a palliative. So that if this bank will have the effect, first, of decentralizing industry, which I am rather doubtful-at all events I express the hope that it may do that-and if it will have the effect of stimulating new industry, then I am going to bless it and wash it Godspeed. But from what we have seen, and from what we have heard from the parliamentary assistant I have faint hopes that such will be the effects. Therefore I ask him and the members on the treasury benches to lay the whole plan of the government before us for full employment in Canada. This is only a piecemeal effort. Give us at the same time what the taxation policy of this country is to be, because that is vital to industry. If you take the returns of industry you will see that to-day it is bearing the great weight of taxation. I know' there are Canadian people who think industry is making millions because they are subscribing millions to victory bonds. Nothing could be more fallacious. Out of what are the subscriptions for victory bonds coming which these industries are subscribing for to-day? I say with certainty that they are coming out of the proceeds of depleted inventories, inventories that cannot be recouped because of the labour situation. The best illustration I know of is the paper companies. Look how the wood piles of the paper companies are depleted. Their inventories have been turned into cash, and the cash in turn has been invested in victory bonds. But when labour is available those bonds must be sold because they are part of the working capital of these companies.
Therefore, in conclusion, I say that to complete the picture we should have not only this feeble step but the government's whole plan laid before us, and I invite the parliamentary assistant to give it to us. In the meantime I am not going to condemn this bill. I am going to adopt an attitude of wait and see.

maintopic: NORTHWEST FIELD FORCE (1885) QUESTIONS AS TO PENSIONS OR OTHER ALLOWANCES
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to follow the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in his argument because I have no doubt that the hon, member responsible for the bill will have something to say to him in reply. I just point this out, that we have heard from him to-night a plea for relief of taxation in the midst of a war in which the people of this country are being called upon to make considerable sacrifices both in men and in resources for the prosecution of the war. But we are told that, if given an opportunity, business is always ready to take a risk. My mind goes back to the period from 1930 to 1939, when there were risks and there were money and resources, but business could not cope with the

situation which we then faced. I say to my hon. friend that as far as we are concerned we welcome the introduction of this measure as a step in the right direction. I would agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury to this extent, that it is indeed a feeble step, but it is a step. A publicly-owned institution of this description is an' attempt, at least, to do something in the way of financing the development of this country by means of a public institution. It is not, in our opinion, adequate to ensure the volume of capital which will be necessary after the war for the promotion of socially desirable industries and for socially desirable purposes. In any event, whatever policy is followed by this industrial bank if and when it is established, it needs to be paralleled by a central bank and a national policy to maintain two things, full employment and adequate purchasing power to distribute the products of industry. In our view, as we have so often said, national ownership and control of the entire banking and financial system is necessary to meet our present problems and solve the problems of the post-war period. But this bank, compared with the matter of the bank charters which we shall be discussing in a few days, in all probability, because the time has now come when we shall have an opportunity of reviewing the bank charters, can be discussed only as a relatively minor measure, for that is what it is. However, we welcome it as a step toward the establishment in this country of a national investment, monetary and credit policy.
There are, however, some criticisms of the bill which I think we should make immediately. First of all, the measure is ambiguous in some respects. We should be sure, before we give it final approval, that the facilities of this industrial bank which we are to set up under this bill will be available not only to what we might call private industry but to cooperative societies which wish to enter into any industrial undertaking, or to any municipal or public enterprise of any sort which wishes to undertake some public industrial or worth-while development of a public nature. Second, we think it should have been accompanied by a measure to establish an agricultural bank in this country. After all, agriculture is a primary and basic industry, and for many years the political parties have been advocating at one time or another the establishment of an agricultural bank. Now we are told that such a measure is under consideration, and I hope that it will be introduced in the near future, so that it may accompany this proposed industrial bank in the statutes of Canada.

Industrial Development Bank
There is another industry which, I think, ought to receive some consideration but which, as far as I can see, is omitted from this bill; I refer to the mining industry-. As I understand it, under existing legislation certain taxation rebates are made for certain works in connection with mining. But it appears to me that the only people who can take advantage of those rebates are the large mining companies, simply because the smaller ones are not in a position to make the kind of profit which enables them to secure the rebates of taxation which will permit them to do the necessary development work. I have always felt that in this country the mining industry is being concentrated into a very few hands; that not more than twenty-five or thirty individuals exercise any real control over the industry; and that the prospectors who do the spade work and discover the resources are, often, those who reap the least reward from the undertakings, which they make possible.
It seems too, and in this I agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury, that this industrial bank may be used merely to assist risky and unprofitable ventures. That should be very carefully guarded against in the administration of this institution, because it would seem-again-that the profitable and more certain ventures will still be taken care of by private lending institutions.
In spite of the demand we hear frequently in this house and across the dominion to give private enterprise another chance, this bill actually removes from the operations of private enterprise any risk whatsoever, or at any rate minimizes it to a veiy great extent. In other words, the argument so often used that we must compensate private enterprise for the risk will, when this institution is functioning, be no longer available to those who are in favour of the complete control of this country by private enterprise. The risk is being minimized, perhaps even removed, and the public are asked to assume that risk which it is said pertains to private enterprise.
Then, it does not begin to lay the foundations for the solution of unemployment, for the provision of full employment. As has already been said, $100,000,000 for industry is an exceedingly small amount in these days. We shall find that we still have unemployment and idle resources-idle, not because there will be after the war, or is even now, a scarcity of savings, but merely because once again industry will be unable to distribute the products of industry. Profit, and not
human need, is the stimulus for production in normal times. One thing the war has taught us, I believe, is that the need of the nation ought to supersede private gain, and that when we are at war we can plan to meet the great public need-far greater-we shall have to meet when we are at peace.
Thus, as I have already said, while the bill is useful in many respects, it is in my opinion quite inadequate. What we need to promote industrial development and to assist purchasing power of the people of this country is a national investment authority together with a planned monetary and credit system, designed to do two things, to produce goods and to distribute them, thus eliminating poverty and raising the standards of living by intelligent and well-defined steps. I said a moment ago that such a policy has been demonstrated as a prime necessity during the war period, and there is no reason why we should not carry the valuable experience that we have had during the war into the peace-time period that will follow. Of course, I do not intend to-night to discuss banking policy under this bill. It does not properly arise under the bill. We shall have an opportunity to discuss banking and monetary policy more particularly when the Bank Act is before the house for revision. Investment policy, however, does arise for the primary purpose of the measure as I see it is to ensure the availability of certain forms of credit-not all forms-to fill a gap to certain types of industry, as we were told when the bill was introduced.
At the moment there are certain main sources to which we look for investment funds. There are the very large accumulations of money in the hands of insurance and trust companies. Then we have the savings of other corporate bodies and the personal savings of the people, and we have of course the undistributed profits of industry. And these undistributed profits, even though we are taxing them in war time, are reaching very sizable amounts.
The private direction of these amounts available to the public and to industry cannot meet the needs of the time. In 1929 there were great accumulations of savings, of investment funds, in the hands of institutions, corporations and individuals; and yet, with all that was available at that time, we entered upon the most devastating period of depression in the history of this country. And then, when we have only private direction of investment, we often have the misdirection of investment funds into all kinds of luxury trades or even into very wasteful expansion. We have
Industrial Development Bank

seen in our day and generation the oil companies adopting the policy of a filling station on nearly every corner, and we have witnessed the overcapitalization of other Canadian industries, such as, for example, newsprint before the depression and before the war. These overdevelopments were costly to the community, and they are more costly because, associated with this form of investment, we have a most wasteful system of securing and placing the funds-investment brokers, syndicates, stock exchanges. Incidentally, that machinery is very largely kept in existence by the public authorities themselves, by governments, federal, provincial and municipal, who go into the market and use the machinery, paying commissions and maintaining the system in order to get the necessary funds for desirable public purposes.
I say that this form of investment control, in the hands of increasingly richer corporations and institutions, is dangerous to the public good. We have heard to-night criticisms of the concentration of wealth and power in certain areas of Canada. We who come from other parts of Canada realize how much truth there is in that criticism. But there is tremendous concentration of wealth in the hands of a few corporations in this country. It is all very well to say that when the war is over we shall deal with some of the great monopolistic corporations that have arisen in our midst; but it is much easier to say that than to break up the great concentrations of power once they have slipped from our control. At the present time we have a great concentration of financial power in a few hands, and I should like to see the government introduce a bill with much wider power than this, so that we might direct investment, not into wasteful channels, into luxury goods, but into housing, into the development of our resources, into the provision of full employment, into the building up of the kind of Canada that most of us believe we could build if we really tried.
The present form of uncontrolled investment results, too, in dangerous fluctuations in our economy. We see a great expansion of credit, investment and so on in a period of inflation, of so-called prosperity; then comes a period of depression, and we have a serious deflation of investment and money. Hence this industrial bank, though we regard it as an inadequate step, is a step perhaps toward something bigger, setting up eventually a national investment board which can direct the savings of our people, of our nation, of our public institutions, as well as of our private citizens into proper socially desirable

channels. But most of all we need this instrument for the purpose of a planned investment, as I have already said, for the securing of maximum employment and to improve generally the economic, cultural and social levels of our people.
A national investment bank instead of a little industrial bank of this description should be incorporated at the present time as a part of our national banking system. . Thus we should have power to use our own national bank of issue more completely than we are able to use it so far. There is no reason why a national investment bank, associated with the national Bank of Canada, the bank of issue, should not in times of deflation, in times of economic recession, issue for capital expansion interest-free money for public undertakings of a desirable sort. Then, if we did strike a period of inflation, that would be the time to get surplus money from the people by borrowing it from them. We should use the financial instrument we now have in order to control our economic structure and our economy in the manner in which it should be controlled in the public interest. Therefore, instead of a bill of this description, which may be merely a prop to private industry, we should have something that would be another real instrument of national policy. That, of course, would mean an institution with much greater capital, with much wider powers than the institution we are discussing to-night.
In the meantime, until we have such an institution, I would suggest to the government that steps should1 be taken to control investment now and in the post-war period so that capital may be guided and directed into socially desirable channels, not to be used wastefully but to raise the levels of our own people. In other words, instead of speculative investment, which is not the proper term; instead of speculation, to put it more correctly, by boards of directors irresponsible in the sense that they are responsible only to their own shareholders, investment should be controlled and directed by an authority set up by and responsible to this parliament or, in other words, respons:ble to the representatives of the people of Canada as a whole. In my opinion such a policy would cheapen the overhead of industrial organizations and assist the community in very many ways.
Therefore, in our opinion the present measure falls short of what should be done at this time; and I say "at this time" advisedly, because while I do not share the view that we could afford, at this critical time, to consider departing from the manufacture of munitions of war and supplies needed by the army

Industrial Development Bank
and navy, yet the time will come when we shall have to consider the provision of consumer goods for the Canadian people in larger quantities. So that I say we should be planning what we should do in those circumstances; we should be laying the foundations now. As I have said, in my opinion this institution to a very large extent destroys the argument that is so often heard in this chamber in favour of so-called free enterprise. It goes some distance in removing the risks for which the public are supposed to pay those who are engaged in free enterprise. As I say, this bill removes their risks, but they will still retain their profits. However, it is a step toward something which I hope will be more beneficial to the Canadian people when we are ready to expand its functions. Therefore we shall support the principle of the bill, and when it is in committee we shall have more to say, in the hope that we may yet widen the scope of the measure in the directions I have indicated.

maintopic: NORTHWEST FIELD FORCE (1885) QUESTIONS AS TO PENSIONS OR OTHER ALLOWANCES
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the principle of this bill is to ensure the availability of credit to industrial enterprises. What is the purpose of the bill? Those who advocate it maintain that it is one of the government's devices for maintaining full employment. If the purpose of this bill is to maintain full employment I must tell the government frankly that they have put the cart before the horse. If this bill is to bring about full employment and guarantee its maintenance it should be entitled something like this: "A bill to ensure availability of money or credit to consumers to enable -them to purchase *the goods which private enterprise stands ready and willing to produce."
What is the haunting fear of private enterprise from coast to coast in Canada, and in fact all over the American- continent? Is it that private enterprise will not be able to produce, that it will not be able to obtain money with which to produce? Not by any means; what private enterprise is worrying about is whether it is going to sell its goods after the war. If private enterprise can sell its goods after the war, private enterprise will employ the people of Canada, just as private enterprise can employ the people of Canada during the war, when the markets are provided by the government purchasing all the goods for use in the war. What is the worry of the farmer, the mining companies, the lumber companies, the milling companies, the factories manufacturing sugar, clothing, shoes, washing machines or anything else? Is it that they will not be able to get money to produce or to expand their capital equipment? Not by 100-81
any means; all -they are afraid of is that they are not going to be able to sell. I have talked with them by the score and they all agree. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated we should be considering ways and means of providing additional purchasing power, not necessarily ways and means of providing additional production. As I have contended on the floor of this house, and as I believe people are coming more and more to recognize, such purchasing power can be provided by the creation and use of debt-free money issued scientifically into the stream of purchasing power in prices, wages, dividends and through other means.
Just to establish my point let us turn to the depression years. What was the cause of unemployment in Canada during the great depression? Was it the fact that people were unable to produce? Was it the fact that industry was unable to obtain money with which to produce? Or was it the fact that industry was unable to sell? Did we suffer from lack of production, or was it overproduction, which of course was underconsumption? If that does not completely establish my thesis I fail to see how it could be established. What caused our trouble during the depths of the depression? We had 750.000 unemployed, more or less; we had 1,250,000 on relief; agriculture was impoverished; labour was living at bare existence levels, and through all we were decreasing and destroying the purchasing power which industry needed in order to be able to sell its goods. Well, if we are going to establish employment in this country we must attack the problem in the right way.
Let us turn to the United States for a few moments and examine the economy of that great nation during the year 1935. What caused unemployment in the United States? Was it inability on the part of industry to produce goods? Not by any means; United States industry, according to Harold Loeb's "Chart of Plenty", stood ready in 1935 to produce enough goods and services to supply every family in the United States with $4,400 worth a year. Were the industries unwilling to produce, I ask my C.C.F. friends? Not by any means. Were they unwilling to sell? Not by any means. Let us get these things straight. I have even heard of some Liberals across the way who apparently have been listening to the socialists and who have begun to be afflicted with the foolish idea that the thing which caused our trouble during the. depression was that industry, for some unaccountable reason, would not produce or would not sell. The difficulty was that they could not sell at a price which would enable them

Industrial Development Bank

to carry on. That was all. What was the situation in the United States, with this capacity to produce $4,400 worth of goods and services for every family in that country during the year 1935? They had between eleven and thirteen million unemployed and about
23,500.000	on relief. Instead of every family in the United States being able to obtain $4,400 worth of goods, only twenty-one out of every 100 people were able to obtain the goods necessary for a bare subsistence, at a decent standard of living.
What was the cause of that trouble? What would have been the remedy? More production? Well, how anyone can get logic out of the contention that it would be more production passes my understanding. If it was more production, then why was it that the President of the United States was causing cotton to be ploughed under, cattle and swine to be shot and thrown into the rivers to go to sea, oranges to be destroyed? It it was a lack of production, then why was all that nonsense going on?
It was a shortage of purchasing power. What we need to be prepared for when this war closes is to supplement the stream of purchasing power in the hands of the people. Will capital expansion provide purchasing power? Some people maintain it will. I maintain it will to a certain extent, but it will not adequately. Where our difficulty lies is in this fact, that machines are displacing men. Consequently many men are no longer able to earn wages as a result of production. At the same time that machines are displacing men, those machines are greatly increasing productive capacity, and produce a vast surplus of goods which, with the present source of income available to human beings, they are unable to purchase.
There is a shortage of purchasing power. Let no one delude himself into thinking that capital expansion will provide the purchasing power necessary to distribute the goods within Canada. If he does, then heaven help the country, if he happens to be in a responsible position, and is in power. Because he will plunge the dominion into a depression worse than the one we had before.
We will grant that a certain kind of capital expenditures might assist. For example, money spent in building vast irrigation projects, vast *reforestry projects, and great road projects, which would supplement the purchasing power in the hands - of the people may, in some degree, provide a remedy. It would do so because it would supply purchasing power without increasing the goods available. But

ordinary capital construction, for instance, in shoe factories or for the purchase of mining equipment and that sort of thing simply will not solve the problem of purchasing power.
Let us examine the bill for a few moments. The declared objective is to help overcome unemployment by providing loans to industry. Will it accomplish that objective? There are certain specific stipulations in the bill, of which this is one:
The bank may establish branches or employ agents in any part of Canada.
Then, No. 2 the bank is to ensure:-*
. . . the availability of credit to industrial enterprises which may reasonably be expected to prove successful, if a high level of national income and employment is maintained.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) I thought discussed that aspect of the bill with considerable effectiveness and success, and therefore it will be unnecessary for me to deal with it.
Then, No. 3:-
The bank may (a) lend or guarantee loans of money to
(i) a person engaged in or about to.engage in an industrial enterprise in Canada.
Then, No. 4:	An industrial enterprise
means:-
A business in which the manufacture, processing or refrigeration of goods, wares and merchandise or the building of ships or vessels or the generating or distributing of electricity is carried on.
These provisions would indicate that the bill has a rather wide measure of usefulness. But there are certain provisos attached to those stipulations which tend in a large degree to nullify the possible effectiveness of the measures to which I have already referred. May I refer to one of these provisos. It states:
.	.	. which may reasonably be expected to
prove successful if a high level of national income and employment is maintained.
May I ask this: By whom may it be reasonably expected? Who is to do the expecting? In other words, how are we to be sure that men who are qualified for credit will be able to obtain such credit? I wonder if the province, through a government agency, or through any other agency, has anything to do with deciding whether or not a company is going to obtain a loan. If the province has no voice at all in this matter, then there will be room for gross discrimination against certain provinces of the dominion.
Will the community concerned have anything to do with deciding who is worthy of a loan, or whether a business is to be classed

Industrial Development Dank
as successful? Who will decide with respect to this matter of success in business? Is allowance to be made for the general economic value to the community, the area, the province or the section generally, in which the industry is supposed to be located? Is allowance to be made for economic value to the community, for example, through employment, markets, aid to other industries, or revenue production?
May I refer to one question which is in the news at this time. It is reported that Ontario is proposing to increase the subsidy on beet sugar production. Why is Ontario proposing to do that? Because Ontario considers the beet sugar industry to be of sufficient value to the economy of Ontario to justify an expenditure, of public money in the subsidizing of that industry.
Is this board which will be approached by industries with requests for loans to be influenced in any degree by the value of the industry, by the value of that industry to the locality in which it is proposed to locate that industry? If it is not, we probably may have a wrong definition of the word "success".
Who is to judge what constitutes a high level of national income? Is this to be the president of the Bank of Canada, or who is it to be? There may be considerable disagreement between the board governing the bank, and the ordinary man on the street, with regard to that matter.
Now then, supposing employment is falling off, instead of being maintained at a high level; is this bill not proposed to be a remedy for unemployment? What conceivable value can the bill have if, at the very time unemployment is setting in, the bank refuses to make loans because there is no possibility of national income and employment being maintained at a high level? It seems to me the sponsors of the bill need to give attention to consistency in their stand.
Then, again, what if national income is falling off? Is it not the purpose of this bill to supplement the national standard of income? And if men who are managing the bank say, as soon .as national income begins to fall, that it will be unsound for the bank to make loans, then obviously there is inconsistency again. The application of this proviso means that as soon as a slump begins, credit from the bank ceases to be available. Let us suppose, for example, that two or three years after the close of the war a slump should set in. Would the bank immediately cease to make loans? Or would those loans be available only for the very strong business? In other words, would they 100-81i
be available only for big business, business which ordinarily is considered to be able to stand on its own feet, without any additional assistance?
If any of the possibilities I have indicated should materialize, the whole purpose of this bank bill would be completely defeated. It would be null and void and useless, as far as the purpose for which it is purported to be designed is concerned. It looks to me, Mr. Speaker, as though this bill is a measure which, when weighed in the balance, will be found wanting, for the purposes for which it is supposed to have been designed. It looks to me as though, under the impact of stern realities, this bank will prove to be unsubstantial, and unequal to its responsibilities.
May I consider the bill from another angle? There is a place into which such a bank could fit. There is a function which it could profitably perform in Canada. Here are some of the possibilities. It could control the banking policy of Canada. We hear a great deal from our socialistic friends, for whom I have high regard, to the effect that it would be impossible to control the banking system of Canada, unless the government owned that system. I challenge that stand, categorically. A bank of the kind we are considering could be used to control the banking policy, even although it were no larger than this bank at the present time. We are proving this in Alberta by the use of our treasury branches. The treasury branch is a relatively weak institution financially, but it has a strong influence upon the financial activities of the province.

maintopic: NORTHWEST FIELD FORCE (1885) QUESTIONS AS TO PENSIONS OR OTHER ALLOWANCES
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext:
That is the important point, the planning of your economy. How would you plan your economy? I maintain you should do it by putting purchasing power in the hands of your people sufficient to enable them to buy your products. There would then
Industrial Development Bank

be no danger of a loss to the banks and the banks would not hesitate to lend money. I believe all hon. members will see that stand is sound and logical.
In direct anstver to my hon. friend's question I would say that if the banks persisted in refusing to lend money, then the thing for the government to do would be to develop an institution of the sort under discussion to dimensions large enough that it could lend adequately. There is no doubt that the government could. This bank is to be provided with $25,000,000 in the form of paid-up capital. That amount could just as easily be $250,000,000. The money will all be created by the Bank of Canada and will cost the Bank of Canada nothing, or it could be so created. Consequently this bank could be expanded by order in council to the point wrhere it would be able to lend all the money necessary in any area of Canada while the banks recovered from their panic.
But the object would not be to have the government go into the banking business. It would be merely to create a corrective to bring the banks into line. Certainly our banks exist to lend money. If they found the government was taking over the lending business I should think they would become concerned about it at an early date and go in and do some lending themselves. We are finding that that is what is actually occurring in Alberta. It must be borne in mind that money can be created debt free. I do not suppose anyone in this chamber will gainsay that. Money can be created regardless of gold. A government can thus be economically and financially free. Let us face that fact realistically and honestly and progressively.
Currency could be created and lent at perhaps one per cent, and credit could be created and lent at perhaps one-quarter of one per cent. If this bank were made a bank of issue, with sufficient support b.y the Bank of Canada, there is no reason why it could not lend credit for working capital, and perhaps currency for fixed capital purposes. This bank could thus be used to control interest rates charged by the chartered banks. The government could control interest rates simply by lowering interest rates on money coming out of this bank. The banks would then have to bring down their interest rates to conform with the interest rates charged by the government-owned institution.
The government could control the availability of loans. If there were men in the community who were worthy of credit but to whom for one reason or another the banks would not provide credit, they could be given
fMr. Blackmore.]
assistance. The bankers would thus be brought into line in a very short time. We have proved that already in many communities in Alberta. For some reason or another banks refuse to lend to certain types of industry in certain areas. A government agency of this kind could lend money to these industries and thus make sure that no discrimination existed. I have in my hand the submission of the government of New Brunswick to the Rowell-Sirois commission in which they complain bitterly of the credit policy in existence in Canada. I believe I will take the time to read a passage which appears on page 49 as follows:
In this connection it is well that the commission should bear in mind that the Canadian banks have been centralized in Ontario and Quebec. Prior to confederation and for some years afterwards we had our own banking institutions in this province and our people were able to obtain money for the encouragement of industry here.
The head office of these banking institutions were removed, after confederation, to Montreal and Toronto where they were situated more immediately in touch with the financial interests by which they were controlled.
The result has been that industries in New Brunswick have not been able to obtain financial assistance in cases where such assistance would enable our local industries to compete with those in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
Pertinent cases may be cited where local industries in this province have been destroyed because of the difficulty of financing and we submit that finances have been withheld as local industries might come into competition with similar industries in the last mentioned provinces.
There has been almost untold suffering throughout seven of the provinces because of the application of that particular principle. That difficulty of discrimination against provinces could be overcome entirely by the government using a bank of this kind. The bankers could be brought into line in the matter of lending to industries no matter in what province they happened to be.
A bank of this sort could control the economy of Canada. We hear a great deal about the decentralizing of industry. Both the hon. members who preceded me referred to the centralizing of industry in Ontario and Quebec and pointed out that it was a bad thing for the Dominion of Canada. Industry should be decentralized and spread out among all the provinces.
A bank of this sort could decentralize industry and render the various provinces of Canada more or less self-sufficient. This would be of great assistance to the maritime and the western provinces. One of the reasons why we in Alberta, Saskttchewan and other prov-

Industrial Development Bank
inces go into debt to the institutions in Ontario and Quebec is the fact that we have not developed sufficient industry. The result is that our people are only primary producers. They are penalized by the low prices they receive and by the high prices they must pay for the products they need. Then they have to pay railroad transportation both ways, and they pay interest upon the money involved in both transactions. If there were an industrial development in each of those provinces it would overcome the tendency of one province to go into debt to another.
A bank of this sort could render Canada self-sufficient to a much greater degree. She would not be obliged to import more than was necessary from abroad. May I point out once more that a bank of this sort can control the banking policy of the Dominion of Canada, doing it by strategic means rather than by ownership. It is not necessary for the government to own the banks in order to control them; control could be exercised by strategic means.
This question must be asked concerning this bank: will these possibilities be realized by this bank? Will interest rates be brought down, and will loans be made available equitably with a view to the greatest good to the greatest number of Canadians? Will industry be decentralized? Will the various provinces be made economically self-sufficient? Will Canada be rendered self-sufficient? Will the banking system be rendered obedient to the government? Will it be made to work for abundance for all, or for scarcity, so that a few may have great profits and power? These are the questions we have to ask ourselves in considering this bill. I fear very much that the answer to every one of these questions is not going to be "yes."
I wonder if the facts which have been adduced already in this debate do not strengthen the suspicion that this bill is nothing but political window-dressing, that it is nothing but a clever device designed to trick the Canadian people into thinking that the King government really mean? to do something to remedy the ill of unemployment, that it does know what to do and that it does have the power to do something effective? I am afjaid that the answer to that must be "yes." It is simply window-dressing. We have had examples of this before in the history of this country. When the Prime Minister spoke of currency and credit in terms of public need in 1935 he led people in the west to think he meant what he said. Then he came into the house a few years later and explained to us very simply that he meant by currency and credit in terms
of public need exactly what we had at the time he spoke. In other words, he had contemplated no change whatsoever. This kind of clever trickery coming from the Liberal party the people of Canada have to be on guard against.
This same man told the people that there would be a -war against the money power waged on the floor of the new parliament. I have been here ever since that parliament convened, and the only war against the money power waged by the Liberal party has been a war for the money power and against those who were trying to control the money power. Never once have 1 seen the government adopt a single measure which would challenge the position of any money power.
Take another example of trickery; we were told that if we had government ownership of the Bank of Canada it would do wonders for us. I ask this question: Did government ownership of the Bank of Canada make any change whatsoever in the banking policy of Canada? Not a bit. I submit to my socialist friends that government ownership of banking institutions without a change in policy will accomplish nothing whatsoever in the interests of the country. But a change of policy, even with private ownership of the banks, will.

If we are to solve the problems confronting us we must use means altogether different from those of which this new bank is an example.
I hold the view that if democracy is to prevail in Canada after the war is won, the government must take fundamental action to change the economic system of Canada from the present system of scarcity into a system of total use of Canada's resources.
The government's task is both a profound and an immensely urgent one. If it is not discharged before the war is won we shall betray our boys fighting on every battle front.
The government has presented a programme of reform. As I have already said, in face of the needs of the Canadian people, the programme is meaningless, just as meaningless as this bill is. It promises much. It can accomplish very little under the present set-up. The reason is that only total use of resources can give the Canadian people the prosperity to which they are entitled, and the fact is that the men behind the government of Canada will not permit the adoption of total use of resources because they believe that only scarcity can pay high profits. And to those concealed advisers and directors of the Liberal party, high profits for them come before prosperity for the people, even if the people should be our boys returning from risking their lives on the battlefield.
To-day there is ample evidence before parliament to prove that the doctrine of scarcity dominates the economy of Canada. Let me give the house one or two examples. Take the meat situation. Hon. members have followed for the last six weeks the development of the meat situation in Canada. Can one conceive of a situation being more pathetically and tragically bungled than- the meat situation in this country? What was the reason? It was simply that the Liberal government does not dare to liberate the productive capacity of Canada, because it fears abundance. It believes only in scarcity at home. Would a bank like this new one that is proposed in any w7ay relieve a situation of that sort? The bank might merely assist the farmers to produce more beef, and the Liberals would be all the more terrified.
Take the sugar situation. I believe solemnly that there has been no need of scarcity of sugar in Canada during this war, or for the years immediately preceding the war, nor has (here been any reason or justification for the
[Mr. Blackmore.J
high prices of sugar which have prevailed. Evidence which I adduced the other night proved conclusively the soundness of my position. I believe that quantity and price have been affected, not so much by the circumstances of war, as by -the fact that prior to the war and also during the war the production and sale of sugar have been manipulated by a sugar trust or combine and that one of the dominating units in this trust has been the St. Lawrence Sugar Refining company. I ask would a bank such as the one we are now considering in any way remedy that situation? Not by any means. How could it? There are plenty of companies that stand ready to finance new sugar refineries to produce beet sugar in this country. Do they need assistance from a bank such as this? Not by any means. All they need is markets. All they need is the go-ahead signal.

I have given one or two examples of the way in which the economy of this country might be influenced and controlled. I have illustrated the way in which huge concerns exercise their influence. I might have added that if it were known whether or not these big concerns which I have referred to have contributed liberally to war loans and if the government feared to disoblige them lest they should desist from lending, it would help us to understand who it is that controls this government and how the control is exercised.
Now may I say to the government that they would escape from all such pernicious controlling influences if they would adopt a sane and sound financial system, one that reflected the facts of the Canadian economy, for no concerns in this country would be able to gain or exercise control over a government which was free to issue money in relation to goods and services such as the people could produce.
May I conclude with both a warning to the government and an appeal? Once more I warn the government that scarcity must give way to .abundance before this war is won; otherwise we shall betray our fighting men. I tell the government solemnly that to-day it should be ashamed to face those boys already coming home from the battlefields. If this government does nothing more than it is doing now, it will be afraid to face our conquering soldiers when the war is won. I say this because upon its performance right up to this date all the government is able to guarantee our soldiers is a return to unemployment and poverty. They are coming home right now to unemployment and poverty, and the trend to such-thousands of them- and nothing is done to alleviate the situation; that is, nothing substantial.
Here is my appeal. I have said that the people of this country have a right to the
total use of their resources. That means maximum consumable production and equitable distribution of that production, distribution by consumption. I defy any man in this house to rise in his place and state that the people are not entitled to this right. I defy any man to say that the people would not have this right if parliament were free to get it for them. Then let us set parliament free. Let the government renounce its hidden bosses and take up the cause of the people. If it does so it will find loyally behind it the membership of this house without regard to party. Then Canada, both French and English-speaking, will give leadership to the English-speaking peoples of the world.
This is a great and holy cause in which we can all serve, this cause of democracy, of freedom from want and fear. Therefore, if the government continues subject'to direction by the hidden hands which have thus far guided it, I appeal to all those patriots in the Liberal party to renounce their party subservience and to join with free men outside the Liberal party to set the people free, and to give a chance to the boys who come home from overseas, and to the parents and loved ones and friends who have saved and served and sacrificed to send them over there.

speechtext:
I want at the outset to say .that I am in favour of sustaining the chartered banks of this country, because I believe they are well controlled and efficiently handled and that they do a splendid service to the people of Canada. Not only do they serve this country, but they operate abroad, and the banking houses of Canada are sentinels in
Industrial Development Bank

foreign countries for Canada's export trade. Wherever I see exports I believe there must be merit, and in order that a country may be a successful exporter to another country there must be strength and workmanship. The superiority which our banking system has maintained for many years will, I believe, stand us in good stead in the years to come, when our export trade will be a big feature in the development of our economic future.
_The Canadian banks are in the vanguard to be factors for our export trade, so that it would not do unduly to interfere with or weaken them. At the same time there is no reason why we should not make an experiment and have an industrial bank as a part of our industrial equipment. We believe in competition and free enterprise, and we must keep abreast of the needs of the time. I trust there is no intention to close the road to any development; rather open it wider to meet the exceptional needs of reconstruction, at this serious period of our history, when all economic forces should be intelligently brought into play. "The government has many statutory provisions whereby special financial consideration is given to our citizens, and it may be that these should be coordinated through a bank. The experiment is worth-while making.
We hear each day a lot of criticism of Canada's war-time effort. Strange to say, most of the praise comes from outside our country. Only to-day I saw in the paper an enthusiastic account of Canada's war effort by a United States commentator, who made the statement that in two years, while Canada's price ceiling had risen two per cent, that of the United States, on the same basis of calculation, had risen fourteen per cent.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury criticized the war effort in speaking of the principle of this bank. Why he had to do that I do not know. I believe that we are progressing in so far as monetary ma-tters'are concerned and that we are keeping up with the needs of the time.
Every one of us, either by reading or by personal experience, remembers the last war. We recall that the money for the conduct of that w'ar was borrowed, whereas in this war we are paying fifty per cent of the cost as we go. During the last war victory bonds were issued bearing 5J per cent interest. This time no such interest is paid. In addition to that, tax-free bonds were sold to the people and there was very little criticism about it at that time. Furthermore, there was no restriction on the accumulation of wealth. Wealth accumulated during the last war; tax-free bonds made it easy for the affluent to pay their taxes, and the percentage paid for borrowing money

was an amount that we would not consider at all in this period of our history. So that we are making progress. While my hon. friend criticizes the action of this government, I believe the statement of the Bank of Canada, which has been presented to this house, shows that in finance Canada has made a splendid and most efficient effort. The statement of that bank, if one considers it calmly, reads like a romance in finance. I think the $15,000,000 profit it has brought to the exchequer of Canada shows that while some people opposed that institution when it was formed, it has a splendid record and engenders enthusiasm and confidence in the Canadian people to go on to other efforts.
The chartered banks of Canada are controlled by law and their activities are in the nature of a revolving cycle; circulation is in and out and it is vital to the success of the country. Frozen loans are avoided wherever possible, because the banks, in the very nature of things, must be kept liquid; they must be able to face the clearing house. Certain business is prohibited. The details appear in section 151 of the Bank Act. Certaain business of a static nature is prevented. This to a degree is the difference between our banks and the banks of the United States. It will be recalled that -the banks of Canada survived the crisis of the last decade while -the banks of the United States met disaster. One factor causing the American difficulties was longterm business. This is the field where present-day conditions seem to show the need, and an- industrial welfare bank is eminently designed for that purpose.
Under section 15 of the act, with respect to business and powers, the bank is enabled to lend or guarantee loans of money to an industrial enterprise, including loans on real or personal property. This is now done largely by trust companies and individuals. . I would say that the bank has some of the characteristics of a bank and nearly all the powers of a trust company, and it is intended to assume some of the functions of both.
I am disappointed that the interpretation section, wherein industry is defined, includes the building of ships but not the operating of ships. It is my opinion that after the war there will be plenty of ships, and the question will be, what are we going to do with them? That will be an important question. There are 80,000 men now in the Canadian navy and 44,498 in the merchant marine. Many of these men will want to continue at sea. I often meet naval officers, especially those of the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve, whose

Industrial Development Bank
ambition is to be part owner of a ship after the war and sail her in the merchant marine trade.
The United States built a number of ships and found them too slow, and now they are building victory ships so as to be in the forefront of the mercantile marine enterprise. It may be that we should build faster ships for the period after the war. In my opinion some provision should be made so that the men on the sea in this war who have great responsibilities in the navy may be able to continue in their calling, and I hope they will get help from their country in order that ships may be operated in. the serious days of reconstruction.
In the prohibited business category in our Bank Act ships are included, and there is also fishermen's floating property along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. Everyone fights shy of lending money on floating property and there is a need which this bank can supply if we so decide in committee. I find that the bill calls for ownership and management by the Bank of Canada. I doubt if this is advisable. It looks too much like a state-controlled monopoly. Erroneously, people have the idea that freedom is embodied in government ownership. Carried to excess, I think it means dictatorship. Competition breeds freedom, initiative and efficiency. I think we all admit that the Canadian National railway service in Canada is better because we have the Canadian Pacific railway, and I recall that Canadian Steamships is an interlocked directorate with Canadian National railways. Well, we lost most of our Canadian ships. It is hard to serve two masters, and in my opinion too much concentration of power in any arm of government is detrimental to the liberty of the subject.
This parliament has had two set-ups of the Bank of Canada. First, this government had a fifty-fifty set-up. whereby the people of Canada owned half the stock and the government the other half. This brought to the Bank of Canada the opinions of men all over the country who were interested in industry. They were elected by the shareholders and we knew what was going on. They had an annual meeting where they had to face the shareholders. It was claimed that the government must own the stock of the Bank of Canada completely to make it effective, because it must supply funds according to public needs, and the act was changed. Will anybody tell you that a person who owns fifty per cent of the stock in any company does not to all intents and purposes control that company? The government controlled that concern, but
they had the advantage of the cooperation of the Canadian public, and while it cost some money in the way of dividends, that could have been controlled.
I noticed one day in the Chateau Laurier, coming down the elevator, a sign on the board: "Annual breakfast of the Bank of Canada." It seems to me that government control is hardly control by the people in its fullest meaning as it was in the original set-up.
It is argued that economies will be effected under this new set-up, but the bill provides that the directors of the proposed bank are to be paid, and they will have an entire managing staff; so why not give them some authority and let the bank stand on its own feet? Let it be strong in its own right. We are told that when we create a company we create another person in law; so let this person be strong. I believe the directors of this bank should be independent of the Bank of Canada;
I think that would be eminently in the interests of the public. For want of a better word I would say that the powers of the Bank of Canada over the banking system of this country are almost judicial. The preamble of the Bank of Canada Act is quite comprehensive; it states that the bank is to regulate currency and credit in the best interests of the economic life of the nation. In section 2 of that act it is provided that the bank shall not, except as authorized by the act, engage m or have an interest in any trade or business. Evidently that provision is to be overcome by forming another company with the same ownership and management.
I am not criticizing, Mr. Speaker; I am only comparing. I note that the proposed bank does not come under the provisions of the Bank Act. That act is for the protection of the people. Under this bill there is no ceiling on business charges. I do not know that this is a serious matter, because they wifi be obliged to be liberal in their dealings in order to carry out the purposes of this bill. We are told that this bank is to help small industries, but there is no ceiling on the amount it can lend to any one company. It seems to me that if we say a bank is intended to help small industries fill the gap that exists in the present lending system, in order to meet the needs of the people, there should be a ceiling so that we may be sure only the small industries wifi be assisted. It may be said that this bank will bring uneconomic forces into play in industry. Well, if we have good management it will be like any other bank, and it is only reasonable to suppose that the management of this bank will see to it that its business is conducted on sound lines. I think I would trust them in that connection.

Industrial Development Bank

and I do not think vve need have any great fear about hurting the chartered banks. They are very strong. Banking in Canada has been remarkably free from competition in the last decade; the banks have cooperated well with each other. In the light of our experience, Mr. Speaker; in the light of the needs of the future, I believe the setting up of this bank is in the public interest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the Chair is for the second reading of the bill to incorporate the industrial development bank. On second reading we may discuss the principle of the bill but not the various clauses. The preamble and the interpretation section describe (he functions of .the proposed bank. Coming from an industrial province and an industrial city, I would hold up both hands in favour of this bill if I thought small industries in this country were going to get any relief from the intolerable artificial burdens and barriers and restraints of trade which have been imposed on small industries by this government since the beginning of the war. Under the control system of Mr. Donald Gordon and his associates on the wartime prices and trade board, $115,000,000 has been the cost of the various bonuses, subventions, subsidies and all that sort of thing, and who is going to pay for them? After all is said and done, in our economy the small industrial man has been the forgotten agency ever since this system of bonuses and subventions was started. I remember when the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was brought in by the former government for the purpose of giving relief to the dirt farmers on the land. In 1935 it was extended to cover fishermen. At that time I contended that relief of this kind should be extended to small industries and to industrial workers throughout the country, but nothing was done. Then came the war, and the government of the day imposed the control system which I have indicated.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) gave a lucid description of the functions of the proposed bank. The hon. gentleman has had a great deal of training, which should equip him for promotion. He stated that one of the functions of the bank would be to prepare the way. Well, they have been a long time preparing the way for the small industries of this country, who have been the forgotten members of our economic state since this war started. This measure is designed to bring about a high level of employment and national income after the war, and according to the preamble the measure is designed to promote
fMr. Kinley.]
the economic welfare of Canada by supplementing the activities of other lenders and by providing capital assistance to industry, with particular consideration to the financing of small enterprises. Then the interpretation clause defines an industrial enterprise. The provisions of this bill are contained in some thirty-four paragraphs; the parliamentary assistant gave a detailed explanation of the scope and object of the legislation. It would appear that the bank has power to guarantee loans, to acquire stock and bonds, and so on, and the bank is given power to lend money to both new and existing industrial enterprises. I should like to find out whether this measure will enable the small business man, who has had to obtain a loan from a shark loan company, to get on his feet again, and transfer to this new bank. Will those who have had to borrow money be helped under this measure? Many of our small industries have had to close up under the present control system.
The proposed bill is a Santa Claus bill. It will be a bank of faith, hope and charity, if it is proposed to aid the small industrial owner. Will the proposed bill enable him to have an account taken with respect to these shark loan companies which are charging him 2 per cent a month and more? Will it enable the small industrial proprietor to go to the subsidiary bank of the government or the Bank of Canada and seek funds from this subsidiary bank of the Bank of Canada in the manner indicated? I say there should be equality of treatment.
The parliamentary assistant said:
I want to make it clear that this bank is intended to supplement the activities of existing lending agencies rather than to displace them. If the credit requirements of a business are of such a nature that they can be obtained from a chartered bank or in the investment market, well and good. On the other hand, if such sources are not available then the industrial development bank will consider applications to assist projects which appear to be economically sound. The industrial development bank is not being set up to finance enterprises which are obviously doomed to end in failure. It would not be in the public interest to subsidize uneconomic activities in this concealed manner. On the other hand if the industrial development bank is to fill the gap I have described, it must operate on the assumption that there will be on the average a relatively high level of economic activity. .	.	. The government
believes that the existence of the industrial development bank will be of particular value to small business which has laboured under a certain handicap in obtaining medium and longterm capital. These small industrial establishments are an essential part of our economy, an important source of employment and production, one which we must not overlook when planning to maintain a high level of employment and income in this country after the war.

Industrial Development Bank
If that is so, namely, that they are an important part of our economy as far as employment is concerned after the war, then it has taken the government of the day nearly five years of war to find it out.
As I say, if this bill is going to give any help to those small industries, then I hold up both hands for it. But when I examine what the facts are I believe that in some respects this is a political bill. In other respects it might turn out to be a Santa Claus bill. Then, it may turn out to be that the industrial owners will not get the same privileges that the farmers, the fishermen and others have received under similar state-aid bills.
In the first place, I think the government in this instance has got the cart before the horse. First of all, it should announce to the house that it is going to remove some of the artificial barriers and burdens in restraint of trade which have been placed upon industry since the beginning of the war. Second, it should announce what its policy is to curb the shark loan companies, those companies which are charging more than two per cent a month. It should also announce what it is going to do about reducing taxation. Many of our industries have found that they have been driven to the wall by the barriers and heavy burdens of taxation.
In addition to that, I find that in England they are preparing for the period following the war. They are taking steps to protect small industry. Over there they have what they call a pre-war trade practices act, to put industry back to where it was before the war. We should have the same kind of bill adapted to our circumstances in Canada.
Perhaps I might point out some of the things which will have to be decided. I believe some of those young gentlemen who are popularly known as the brain trust or theorists who are behind the finance department, those men who have been the framers of the bill, as I see it, have not yet had any practical training in any competitive business. Yet we find them imposing in an unrestricted fashion these artificial burdens and barriers on business. Before the government creates this subsidiary bank it should make some announcement of policy. What is its policy going to be with respect to the proposal of one leftist party to take over the banks and the insurance companies? In my opinion, an election should clear the air and we should first decide whether or riot we are to have a totalitarian state, because if we are to have that there will be no such thing as private industry or private enterprise, or any large industry or small industry in Canada. That is one of the first things which will have to be decided.
We must decide, further, if we are to have tariffs. I know of no businessman to-day, either in large or small industry, who will invest a dollar in the expansion of his industry until he knows what the electors of Canada will do with the proposal to create a totalitarian state, a state in which the banks and insurance companies will be taken over.
In Ontario, during the term of office of the Drury government in 1923, a proposal was made along the lines of free trade with our competitors and destruction of industry. During the four or five years that government was in office not a business man in Ontario would invest one dollar in any industry. The result was that many industries were driven to the wall.
A decision will have to be made on what is to be done about preferential tariffs, which are guaranteed by article 4 of the Atlantic charter. What is to be done about that? What is to be done with preferential and favoured nation agreements. And, by the way,
I should like to get some attention from the ministry for a short time. For the past three years I have been asking the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) what is to become of industry after the war. I should like very much to have their attention, particularly that of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. It is not often I address a question to him, and I do so now in all seriousness. In the sessions of 1941, 1942 and 1943 I proposed that the minister should make an announcement as to what he is going to do, when the war ends, with large and small industries in Canada working on war contracts with the government. It took many years after the last war before business could convert from a war-time to a peace-time economy. Money was not advanced under the Bank Act, and business was tied up, causing widespread unemployment. I presume this bill will be sent to a committee, but before it goes we should have some announcement from the government as to its policy on the matters I have raised, and a statement as to how much money it will release. I suggest that it should be up to fifty per cent, and that there should be some standard form of accounting taken immediately in ail industries, so that when the time comes for a cessation of hostilities business men who could not get advances from the chartered banks on a standard plan might get it through some government policy ahead, instead of having to wait three or four years or, as happened after the last war, sometimes ten or fifteen years, to get some help and settlement of accounts here.
Industrial Development Bank

In my opinion small industry has been done to death by controls, subcontrols, artificial burdens and barriers put upon them by the wartime prices and trade board. Many of them have, had to close up, because they could not get the labour or deliveries of parts of machinery. They were the victims of the system.	.
We find that this proposed bank contracts itself out of the Bank Act. Provision is made in the bill with respect to loans on real estate. A coach and four has been driven by some of the larger chartered banks as to real estate clean through section 82 of the Bank Act. Not by the widest stretch of imagination can it be said that, any chartered bank in Canada to-day has power to go into commercial real estate. I should like to have the attention of some of the members of the treasury board who are here this evening, because they are responsible for the present violation of section 82 of the Bank Act which has enabled these banks to go into commercial real estate. The government are writing into this industrial development bank bill the same power given to the chartered banks, I believe by sections 22 and 23. Section S2 of the Bank Act reads:
No bank shall hold any real or immovable property, howsoever acquired, except such as is required for its own use, for any period exceeding seven years from the date of the acquisition thereof, or any extension of such period as in this section provided, and such property shall be absolutely sold or disposed of, within such period or extended period, as the ease may be, so that the bank shall no longer retain any interest therein unless by way of security.
They were not to go into commercial real estate except for the purchase of buildings necessary for their business. The section continues:
2.	The treasury board may direct that the time for the sale or disposal of any such real or immovable property shall be extended for a further period or periods, not to exceed five years.
3.	The whole period during which the bank may so hold such property under the foregoing provisions of this section shall not exceed twelve years from the date of the acquisition thereof.
4'. Any real or immovable property, not required by the bank for its own use, held by the bank for a longer period than authorized by the foregoing provisions of this section shall be liable to be forfeited to His Majesty for the use of the Dominion of Canada: provided that
(a)	no such forfeiture shall take effect until the expiration of at least six calendar months after notice in writing to the bank by the minister of the intention of His Majesty to claim the forfeiture; and
(b)	the bank may, notwithstanding such
notice, before the forfeiture is effected sell or dispose of the property free from liability to forfeiture.	y

5. The provisions of this section shall apply to any real or immovable property heretofore acquired by the bank and held by it at the time of the coming into force of this act.
Notwithstanding all the provisions contained in the Bank Act for inspection and auditing and all that sort of thing, we had the failure of the Home bank and the Farmers' bank. What is to happen in connection with this industrial development bank? I do not want to throw cold wrater on the idea because I want to see a real bank that will give relief directly and indirectly to the small industries of this country to put them on their feet. They have been the forgotten agencies and we shall have to have some declaration of policy from the government on the various matters I have mentioned. Until that is done I do not think we can express an opinion on the functions or *the objects or the proposals in connection with this industrial development bank.
There are one or two other matters I should like to raise in connection with this bill. What is to be done with the loans already arranged for with different small shark loan companies set up by the Department of Finance, which are charging over two per cent a month? Are the small industries to be given the same privileges which were granted under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to farmers and fishermen? Are these loans to be taken over by the industrial development bank? I know many small industries in my city have been driven by war and controls to the wall; there are three or four in my own industrial riding. There has been no retrenchment in taxation and I do not know how the business man is to continue with the present state of affairs.
When dealing with another matter I referred to a visit made by Mr. Morgenthau, the treasurer of the United States, to Italy. He saw some of the soldiers over there who had had individual small businesses before they enlisted. They wanted to know if in addition to suffering in flesh and blood they were to be asked, when they returned, to pay for the war as well. They wanted to know if they were to get back their small businesses. Something should be done to provide relief for these small businesses. I cannot see anything in this bill that will protect the soldier who had a small individual business and who left it in the care of his wife or some other relative. They should be able to apply to the bank for relief.
The minister is not here this evening, but his parliamentary assistant has described the bill. This country was built up largely by our industries and since confederation they have paid a large share of the taxes. They have had little or no protection from the

Industrial Development Bank
controls and artificial barriers which have been imposed since the war started. I hope that when this bill goes to the committee the small men-I am here to represent the small retailer and business man-will be able to get some relief which he is not getting to-day.
