speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that there will be general agreement with the purpose of this bill as expressed in the preamble, which states:
Whereas it is desirable to establish an industrial development bank to promote the economic welfare of Canada by increasing the effectiveness of monetary action through ensuring the availability of credit to industrial enterprises which may reasonably be expected to prove successful if a high level of national income and employment is maintained, by supplementing the activities of other lenders and by providing capital assistance to industry with particular consideration to the financing problems of small enterprises.
The bill proposes the setting up of an institution which is to be owned and controlled by the Bank of Canada and which may lend or guarantee loans to any industrial enterprise. As I understand it, capital will be supplied to the extent of $25,000,000 by the Bank of Canada, and a further $75,000,000 will be provided by permitting the industrial bank to borrow money on bonds or debentures. There is a provision that when the reserve is built up to the extent of another $25,000,000 from profits, the bank can borrow on bonds and debentures a further $75,000,000. The extent of the capital at present available, however. would be $100,000,000.
I should think one of the main purposes of the bank would be to assist those returning from overseas to get established in small businesses. I believe it will be acknowledged that one of the difficulties encountered by anyone starting up in business who has to borrow money on long term is the interest burden. It seems to me that the rate of interest to be charged should not exceed three or three and one half per cent. That brings up one of the features of the bill which I submit should be reconsidered, and I hope the banking and commerce committee will reconsider it.
Once the $25,000,000 advanced by the Bank of Canada is used up, the remaining money will have to be obtained, under the set-up proposed by this bill, by selling bonds or debentures. Those bonds or debentures, in order to meet a ready market would have to bear interest, I suppose, of around 4^ or 5 per cent. Mr. Towers, the governor of the Bank of Canada, in giving evidence before the banking and commerce committee in 1939 estimated that it cost two per cent of the assets of the chartered banks to do business.
Assuming that the cost of doing business by this bank would be in the same proportion

it might be higher because it would not be business on the same scale as the chartered banks to begin with-they would have to lend money at around seven per cent. They could not possibly hope to lend money at less than six per cent, and I submit that in order to help small businesses provision should be made for them borrowing money for a long term at not more than 3i per cent. In order to make that possible two things could be done. In fact, both I submit should be done. One is to permit the bank to receive deposits on which it would not have to pay more than 1 or 1-J per cent. The other would be to permit the bank to make use of the rediscount privileges which the chartered banks now have. In other words, it should have the right to take its bonds and rediscount them with the Bank of Canada at the present rediscount rate of li per cent and, if the rate were lowered, at the going rediscount rate.
The chartered banks have consistently taken the stand that if they are not permitted to make loans or to purchase government securities to the extent of ten dollars for every one dollar of their cash reserves, they cannot extend credit at the present rate of interest which they have to charge, which in many cases is six and seven per cent. I submit that if the chartered banks have to charge six and seven per cent with the privilege of accepting deposits and having the rediscount privilege, this new bank without such privileges would have to charge even more. The industrial development bank should be allowed to accept deposits the same as any chartered bank and have the same rediscount privileges. To deprive it of those privileges would be to force it to charge a higher rate of interest than it should if it is to carry out the function for which it is being set up.
As to the bill itself, I naturally will support it because I think it is a definite step in the right direction. It has been said that the bill does not go far enough. I remember when this government came into office in 1936 it found in existence a Bank of Canada which was owned and controlled by private interests, and it brought in a bill whereby it took control of the Bank of Canada but left the private interests owning the same number of shares in the Bank of Canada that they owned before and left them with representation on the board of directors. In other words, the private interests were left with a substantial ownership of shares in the Bank of Canada and a substantial share of control of the bank. It was suggested at that time that because the
Industrial Development Bank

government had not introduced a bill to establish one hundred per cent ownership and control by the public of the Bank of Canada we should vote against the bill, but my attitude at that time was this. I was not going to vote against a step in the right direction just because it did not go as far as I should have liked it to go.
My attitude in regard to this bill is the same. I do not think enough capital is provided to do the work, but that can be remedied as more and more capital is acquired. I do not think the bill provides for getting the capital at a low enough cost. That should be remedied in the banking and commerce committee; if it is not remedied in that committee it will become very plain in the actual operations of the bank that it should be done, and it will be done at any rate when the bank has had a chance to operate for a short time.
I certainly am pleased that it is proposed to introduce a bill to provide for cheaper long-term credit to the farming industry. Anyone who has watched the development of the farming industry in western' Canada will, I think, agree with me when I say that one of the great difficulties of that industry has been the fact that the farmers have had to pay seven and eight, and nine per cent on mortgage loans. Had those loans borne interest at around three per cent, then pay-[DOT] ment of eight per cent over a period of less than twenty years would have paid the loans off. But what happened was that in fairly prosperous years the farmers paid the eight per cent and were unable to cut down the principal of the loans, and that when times got a little worse they found the loans too heavy to carry, and the fact that they had to pay interest on these loans cut down their standard of living to a very low level. So that I think it is all important that steps be taken to lower the cost of money to the farming industry.
It is also very important that the agricultural bank when set up will have the right to accept deposits and have the right of rediscount so that it will get its money at least as cheaply as the chartered banks get theirs. If it gets its money as cheaply under the rediscount privilege at 1 t per cent, and assuming that it takes two per cent to do business it could lend money at 3| per cent to farmers to improve their homes and buildings, to get implements, to electrify their homes, and perhaps get better breeding stock.
A bill like that I hope is in the mind of the government and will be enacted this session 
It has been suggested that all of the government's programme should be put before the house at once. But my answer to that Would be that such a programme has to be put before the house step by step. It can all be considered in the banking and commerce committee as a whole, unless the committee decides that it wants to report each item separately.

The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) availed himself of this opportunity once more to indicate, as I took it, that if the government took control of industry in this country there would be no difficulty at all. Mr. Speaker, as I was saying when interrupted by the hon. member for AVeyburn, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation suggest that if they take control of all industry in this country and ownership of all the means of wealth production in the country, they would have no difficulty in regard to handling the situation in Canada. I would say in that regard that, whether the state owns and controls industry or whether it does not, if we have not the markets to export the vast surpluses of food products, metal products and wood products which we produce, there will be great difficulty in handling the industrial and economic set-up,
Industrial Development Bank

and the fact that it is owned by the government will make it no easier to meet the situation than if it is handled by private industry. It seems to me that in advocating that a group of politicians should control the industrial set-up, instead of having it controlled by the people who are used to it, and without meeting the problem of markets, the C.C.F. are taking for granted that the Canadian people have very short memories and very little understanding as to how these things do actually operate.
Another matter which has been mentioned, and which I think is of importance, is the decentralization of industry. I have felt for some time that banking policy shows more unwillingness to extend credit to industries in the maritimes and in western Canada than to industries in Ontario and Quebec. I suggested some years ago that there should be some means whereby anyone who had a good proposition and was denied credit to develop it should have a right of appeal to some body which would have in mind the interest of the country as a whole. It is true that to-day the banks, in extending credit, consider only banking interests, and it is time that there should be some control over them in the extending of credit, so that, should they allow the interests of the banks too much weight as contrasted with the best interests of the country, there should be some public authority able to intervene.
We have a board of grain commissioners. It is suggested that we have a board of live stock commissioners. I submit that in handling a public franchise as important as public credit there should be an authority to which people or, indeed, communities, could appeal if they did not think they were getting a square deal. I suggest that, if we retain our present banking system substantially as it is, there should be a board of bank commissioners to which people could appeal if they did net get a square deal with respect to the extension of credits.
As to the necessity for providing for cheap long-term credit, I would give an example. One of the things we need badly in western Canada is mills to crush flax and oil-bearing seeds, which we grow. It would save the cost of shipping them east, and it would retain to us the by-products which we can obtain from crushing these plants. As I understand it, there is great difficulty in getting credit to set up these oil-crushing plants because, most bank directors being stationed in the eastern and central part of Canada, they know only the set-up in their own areas and are less inclined to advance credit to industries on the prairies

or in the maritimes. This bank, I assume, will enable people who want to set up such oilcrushing plants to get the necessary credit. It comes down to this, and I am quite frank to say so, that the banks to-day operate the most valuable franchise which this country has given to any group of people, and that franchise must be operated in the interests of the people of Canada; otherwise either they will have to be controlled or, as the other alternative, the franchise will be taken away from them. As a Liberal I believe it would be much better to control the banking system in the best interests of the country, rather than put it in the hands of politicians to operate under the control of a government.
I am quite satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party, when they take the attitude that the government should control everything, are proposing a policy whereby ultimately the government would be so powerful that political liberty would become a fiction. I have no doubt that if a government got control of the entire economic activity of the country our political rights would go. I suggest, therefore, that the solution consists in steps such as this by which, to the extent required, we may improve our economic system so that it shall meet the needs of the time without transferring to the hands of a government the ownership and control of industry except as absolutely required by the needs of the time as developments occur.

speechtext: Speaking on my own behalf only, may I say definitely that there is no restriction on the rights of the government. There is no power on the part of the opposition to prevent the government from going into supply. There is no obligation either of rule or of procedure to prevent the government from calling any items of supply that may be entered into.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: NORTHWEST FIELD FORCE (1885) QUESTIONS AS TO PENSIONS OR OTHER ALLOWANCES
speechtext: The minister cannot mean that in the manner in which he says it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: NORTHWEST FIELD FORCE (1885) QUESTIONS AS TO PENSIONS OR OTHER ALLOWANCES
speechtext: I certainly do.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: NORTHWEST FIELD FORCE (1885) QUESTIONS AS TO PENSIONS OR OTHER ALLOWANCES
speechtext: After all, we are willing that the government should get into supply in each of these cases, but if the government invites an amendment each time it asks for supply, then of course we shall be inclined to oblige them with an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: NORTHWEST FIELD FORCE (1885) QUESTIONS AS TO PENSIONS OR OTHER ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
We called two items on Monday afternoon to give an opportunity for amendments or discussion according to the desire of any group in the house.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Ralston the house adjourned at 10:55 p.m. until Thursday, at three o'clock p.m., pursuant to special order made Monday, February 21, 1944.
